consent.title: Usage analytics
consent.intro: OnlineCV has no backend — your CV is stored only on this device and is never uploaded.
consent.tools: Even so, to understand how the app is used and where it fails, usage data is collected through Google Analytics, Microsoft Clarity and Yandex Metrica: the pages you open, the buttons you press, your device and browser, your approximate region, and a replay of your session in the interface.
consent.recorded: The session replay records the interface while you fill the CV in, so the details you type can appear in it. The CV file itself is never uploaded and stays on this device; recordings are used only to find and fix problems.
consent.declined: No analytics tool was loaded and nothing is being sent. You can keep using the app, but the errors you run into will not reach us and cannot be found and fixed — you are using the app at your own risk.
consent.statusGranted: You have allowed usage analytics on this device.
consent.reloadHint: Reload the page for the change to take full effect.

welcome.title: Shall we show you around?
welcome.body: A short tour points out every button in the editor — how to change the design, choose the CV language and download the PDF — and says briefly what belongs in each section.
welcome.hint: You can leave at any time. This is offered only once; afterwards the tour stays inside the guide.

steps.templates: {{templates}} designs to choose from — with a photo or without, one column or two. Pick one and the preview changes at once, and you can switch as often as you like.
steps.preview: Your CV exactly as it will be downloaded, updating as you type. Watch this pane when you try a different design.
steps.cvLanguage: The language the CV itself is written in: headings and values picked from lists follow it. It is separate from the language of the app, so you can fill in an English CV in your own language.
steps.uiLanguage: The language of the app. It does not change the language of your CV.
steps.export: Downloads the finished CV. The PDF holds real text rather than a picture, so the systems employers use can read it.
steps.backup: Saves your data as a file. Nothing is kept on a server, so this file is the only way to move your CV to another browser or device.
steps.reset: Empties everything and starts a new CV. It is not an undo — without a backup file the data cannot be brought back.
steps.help: The full guide: what every field wants, and how to write a CV that gets read. Each section below also has a question mark of its own.

sections.basics: Your name, photo, date of birth and a few lines about yourself. Fields you leave empty — or hide — simply do not appear on the CV.
sections.contact: Phone numbers, email and profile links. Each channel gets its own icon, so a mobile is told apart from a WhatsApp or Telegram number.
sections.experience: Where you have worked and what you did there. The newest job goes first automatically — the order is worked out from the dates.
sections.education: Schools, colleges and universities. Start typing and the list suggests institutions.
sections.certifications: Courses and certificates, with who issued them and when. Add the link if the certificate can be checked online.
sections.skills: The skills you want to be found for, each with a level from 1 to 100.
sections.languages: The languages you speak, from A1 to C2 or as a native speaker. A language that is not on the list can simply be typed.
sections.projects: Work worth showing that was not a job — your own products, open source, freelance.
sections.interests: A few interests, a word or two each. Optional, and the first thing to drop if the CV runs long.
